I also self host some services: keycloak, forgejo, home assistant, immich, grafana/prometheus, jellyfin, pureftp (to store my surveillance cameras videos), and a vibecoded financial app, and soon hermes agent on a 2023 laptop.
I chose to run most of them on Kubernetes since I am used to work with it. I use:
- ha-proxy running on the host and istio running inside the cluster for the sni based ingress routing
- cert-manager with a self-signed CA I had to import the CA cert on my devices
- cloudnative pg for postgresql dbs (keycloak and immich)
For the backup it is mainly some cron jobs that save to the cloud.
It is overkill I admit but kubernetes makes some integrations easier. Even though it was also a way for me to maintain some Kubernetes skills for my work. The tricky part is the network connectivity, for instance home assistant runs inside the cluster on its own network and it makes things more complex like homekit bridge integration (different network than my devices). But with the help of AI the iptables configuration makes wonders.
The kubernetes cluster is k3s running on NixOS micro vms, fully managed declaratively thanks to NixOS.
The services that run outside the cluster (ha-proxy, jellyfin) are all managed declaratively.
At some point I had thought of using proxmox with lxc but I am very happy with NixOS.

I use Yggdrasil [0] to connect my computers.  This ensures they are always connected within a flat, private IPv6 namespace.  However, two computers cannot find each other if they are both behind NAT on different networks.  At least one of them must be reachable by the other via TCP.  That’s why I use the cheapest VPS I could find as a globally accessible Yggdrasil hub.  I’ve been running it this way for many years now, and it works flawlessly.  I can even assign names for the IPv6 addresses using regular DNS, which makes things very convenient.
I also run a few personal web services: Immich, Gitea, Bookstack, Jellyfin, and more.  That cheap VPS couldn't handle it.  I run the services on a computer in my home office.  Caddy runs on the VPS with one proxy line per service.  Data is, of course, exchanged via Yggdrasil.  The domains for the various services all map to the VPS’s IP addresses.  Caddy then handles the routing correctly.  The system works simply.  I can even run storage-intensive services like Jellyfin, and it only costs me a few euros for the VPS.
[0] https://yggdrasil-network.github.io/

There are two themes in this article that end up both being flawed:
- Proton’s not an honest/forthright company in terms of open source and for-profit status
- Proton is flawed technically and isn’t really encrypting your data.
Starting with the former, I think the author is letting perfect get in the way of good. Proton has a whole lot of open source going on with their products and that is a whole lot more than anyone else in the space considering the breadth of their products. I don’t blame the author for misunderstanding some complicated technical concepts, but they are sound concepts.
Yes, a service like this needs to make money to be viable long-term. Having a non-profit parent company is way better than being a public company with public shareholder pressure or being owned by Bain Capital.
As far as the second theme here, the author is just plain mistaken on Proton’s encryption. The author is just misunderstanding the technical aspects of the services and goes further than that by accusing Proton of AI marketing copy, which I am personally not seeing. It looks like normal, sensible, and pretty easy to understand writing to me. I can understand if these concepts are difficult to grasp for the general public but I’m not seeing any problems, and there’s also a lot of third party auditing transparency as well.
It might be nice if Proton offered a more user-friendly alternative to PGP encryption for non-technical non-Proton email recipients, like using some kind of secure temporary link inside an unencrypted email, but also, Proton doesn’t have to be the one to provide that service. The author is asking Proton to do the impossible and fix the flaws of email. And you still have a really nice benefit that every Proton user you email has e2e encryption baked in. There’s really no other service with as significant  user base offering that.
The author goes on to accuse Proton of spreading themselves too thin despite having a really strong product portfolio. There’s really nothing that their apps are missing besides strong photo organization in Proton Drive similar to something like Ente, Google Photos, iCloud Photos, Immich, etc. They’re pretty much a one-stop shop for everything you could want and are a drop-in replacement for big tech cloud suites with a very respectably better privacy footprint.
Finally, I’ll address the political bit even though I shouldn’t: I’ll just say that a company’s CEO having opposite political beliefs of you is a very legitimate reason to not patronize that company. If the author feels like they can’t be a Proton customer because of public statements made by the CEO, good on them. That’s why CEOs pragmatically shouldn’t talk in a partisan way so they don’t alienate customers. With that said, good luck finding a company with a CEO who isn’t right-leaning. Gopher is a self-hosted, open-source version of Cloudflare Tunnel. It turns one public IP into as many as 65k public services by using L4 tunnels from your machines to the edge, rather than traditional L3 routing.
  photos.yourdomain.com → router.yourdomain.com:1024 →Immich on home NAS (192.168.1.50:2283)
  lab.yourdomain.com → router.yourdomain.com:1025 → Jupyter on uni wifi (10.0.10.34:8888)
  vault.yourdomain.com → router.yourdomain.com:1026  → Bitwarden(192.168.56.8:8000)

Hi HN, I’m Alex. I built Gopher over the last seven months.
Background: Pre-2025, UCLA used to give every device and VM on eduroam a public IPv4 address (perks of “inventing the internet”, i guess). Incredibly insecure, but as a freshman in college getting into infrastructure and just having bought my first homelab node, it was an absolute blessing.
However, in 2025, they moved to NAT overnight. Instantly all of my servers I had been running for myself, my research lab, and our ACM chapter lost external access. Now the default answer would have been Cloudflare tunnels, but not only was our DNS not on CF, doing so would have involved letting Cloudflare terminate your TLS and see every byte of our traffic in plaintext, which felt like it was defeating the point of self hosting.
Hence, I built Gopher. It’s a single Go binary on a box with a public IP (ideally self-hosted, but realistically a VPS - mine’s on OCI). Origin servers dial outbound to the edge over rathole with Noise transport, so even though we have zero control over the routers (we couldn’t even get a private IP subnet… let alone public IP), we can expose service without an open port or static IP. I mean if you really tried, you could run a server on the coffee shop wifi down the street - not that I would recommend you attempt to.
Caddy on the edge handles TLS termination and L7 subdomain routing. Because the edge decrypts TLS, it can actually filter requests, there's a JS proof-of-work challenge with HMAC-signed session cookies that drop scrapers before they hit the origin, plus password-gated routes. There’s so many possibilities here; the next logical step would be caching (think CDN).
A big distinction from the self-hosted tunneling space (Tailscale, Netbird, etc) is that Gopher is targeted for public services, not private access.This is for things like a membership portal, where users can’t be expected to install a VPN just to access it - it’s zero client configuration access.
Today is the first stable release (v0.1.0). Now to be candid, while it’s been running our ACM chapter’s infra for 6 months (25 services, no incidents), I wouldn’t put it behind an SLA yet. Frankly, I’m the only contributor, and something of this scope needs more eyes and deployments before it has reached that level.

You can use our Desktop app[1] or CLI[2] to export your data, incrementally. There's a toggle within our Desktop app that will perform this operation continuously into a directory of your choosing. You can of course script the CLI however you'd like.

Deduplicating by SHA (so, exactly the same bytes) is straightforward, and phototprism does that: https://docs.photoprism.app/user-guide/library/duplicates/
Unfortunately, if you've used Google Takeout or other systems that can both downsample your photos and videos, as well as actually deleting _or changing_ metadata, deduplicating becomes a big wad of heuristics.
My first approach was to build a UID based on a series of metadata fields (like captured-at time, the shutter count of the camera body, and the geohash), but that breaks when metadata is missing or edited from their sibling variants.
Just finding what assets to compare against by time proved to be problematic in some edge cases. By storing in UTC (which is how I've built systems for the last thirty years!) made any file that didn't encode a time zones be wrong by whatever the correct offset was--almost all videos, and many RAW file formats don't have timezones. The solution I came up with was to encoding captured-at time _in the local time_, rather than  UTC. I also infer or extract a milliseconds of precision for the date stamp, so files with more or less precision will still overlap during the initial captured-at query.
If you're interested, more details are here: https://photostructure.com/faq/what-do-you-mean-by-deduplica...
My main point here is to expose how deep this rabbit hole goes—I'd suggest you think about these different scenarios, and how aggressive or conservative you want to be in duplicate aggregation, and what you want to do with inexact duplicates.
Most importantly: have full offline backups before you use any deduping or asset management system. When (not if) the tool you're using behaves differently from how you expected, you won't have lost any data.

Terrible Photo Backup App

The primary purpose of a backup is to restore data from it. However, in practice, Immich is horrible at restoring photos to your phone. Consider this scenario: you purchase a new iPhone and use your own Immich server to back up your old iPhone’s photos. You want some of those photos on your new iPhone, so you open the Immich app, connect it to your new phone, and press the download button on a few photos to create a wallpaper on your new iPhone. Surprisingly, the app is coded so poorly that it doesn’t exclude the photos you restored or downloaded from Immich to your new phone. As a result, you end up with duplicates on the Immich server when the auto-backup begins from your new iPhone. It only excludes those photos once it backs them up again.

I conducted some research and discovered that someone had submitted a feature request on the Immich GitHub to “Prevent re-upload of downloaded photos during app backup task.” The maintainer, bo0tzz, responded to them by suggesting that you should exclude the download album from your backup selection. However, this solution is invalid. Once you exclude the download album, you won’t be able to backup any photos saved from Safari or any other app. The app is stupidly designed to only exclude photos it backs up rather than also excluding the restored photos you download from it.

I'm surprised nobody else has mentioned it, but I recommend going with an Intel processor (8th gen or newer). This gets you Intel QuickSync (hardware video encoding/decoding) and an integrated GPU, making 4K video transcoding/playback a breeze. This opens up possibilities like Jellyfin, Frigate, and improves performance significantly for Immich.

I've got an i5-8500T (no external GPU) that's managing 6x always-on security cameras in Frigate and Jellyfin streaming for 6 family members (local and remote with transcoding), plus a dozen other docker containers for Home Assistant/websites/*arr stack plus 4 always-on Linux VMs for various other projects, and the CPU sits anywhere from 30-60%. It's amazing how capable old CPUs are as long as they have hardware video codecs.

Your biggest concern is going to be RAM. The more things you want to run on the server at once, the more RAM you'll need. I need 64GB for my above stack for example.

I think a used laptop or NUC-style mini PC is a great choice for a starter setup! Especially something with onboard soldered RAM, because this will be somewhat immune to the current RAM pricing crisis. If you can force the laptop battery to only charge to 50% in BIOS, you get a free UPS with little risk of battery death. You can always migrate to something more permanent/expensive if you enjoy the hobby.

Retired business or surveillance hardware is worth checking locally too. My two servers are repurposed NVRs running plain Ubuntu Server, and a Dell OptiPlex handles dev work. For that list, I'd start with the hardware you can get affordably and check its RAM capacity and drive connections before buying. Docker on plain Linux keeps things straightforward. I'm in the process of switching off the apple ecosystem and my main learning so far has been to go slower than you think, change is hard and time consuming. I recommend the following.  

**1) Switch one thing at a time**  

I made the mistake of buying new devices before I had switched any service providers. This meant I had to switch and test a new os and multiple new services simultaneously, which was extremely stressful. Switching one thing at a time means the process takes longer but is more likely to keep her motivated and engaged.  

**2) Plan what to change and the order of the steps**  

It will help her motivation if she has a goal and knows why she is changing something, particularly if she can find a reason other than just platform compatibility. Think about things like cost, privacy or ethical considerations, practicality of services you two (would like to) share e.g. calendars, shared albums.  

Timing also matters. First priority is those services which have compatibility issues with android and/or linux, for which you will need to find a cross-platform alternative. Other services she might only choose to change after switching her OS, to options that aren't available in the apple ecosystem.  

Start with the services she uses a lot or which have strong emotional value. If you can't switch those, the experiment is over.  

**3) Osxphotos for faces**  

Apple photos does not have the option to export a lot of metadata. Particularly relevant for me was that no information on faces is exported, which is something I spent a lot of time on. I switched my photos to Ente, using their recommended approach directly on my iPhone, and none of that metadata transfered.  

I recently discovered Osxphotos (on github), which lets you export all the metadata on a mac. That's actually next on my to do list - export my photos on my mac and reimport them to Ente.  

**4) Setup the new os in parallel**  

Install Linux on a partition on her mac, so that she can switch between MacOS and Linux. That gives you time to work out any issues. If she likes it, she will naturally start using Linux more, until eventually it becomes her daily driver.  

**5) New hardware comes last**  

Hardware is expensive and it sucks to spend money and then feel like you have to use something which you don't really like. So use linux on her mac and consider buying a 2nd hand phone to test and play with before switching her sim.  

**6) Be careful of dependence**  

Be careful of self-hosting too much for her. Think about what happens if you're not around for any reason (accidents happen) and ensure she has a good plan and knows how to access and transfer her data from self-hosted to alternative options. That's why I prefer Ente to Immich.  

Also, if your self-hosted services go down at a critical time for her, that could be bad for your relationship.

I tried this in my homelab, and I wanted to convert my Proxmox with it's LXC's over to it...but the problem I ran into was that it was a little too obtuse for what I wanted to use it for.

Long story:

I wanted to get away from Proxmox as a platform and LXCs in general over to another hypervisor and using standard containers. I was tired of having a full fat web GUI to manage things with. Yes you can use pct and other CLIs tools in Proxmox to get some speed, but you are still dealing with an opinionated, dare I say proprietary stack.

Incus is really cool in that it's CLI driven first, and you can add a GUI later if you want. I thought that was nice, and I was able to get some VMs started in my lab cluster and get clustering kinda working. I thought I was in a good place to switch.

But then, my main file server died (thankfully just the mobo, not the ZFS disks). And I was scrambling to figure out how to get all of my functionality back without having to go back to adding the storage back to Proxmox. So I took it as an opportunity to go to incus. 

Well it turns out, it's not so turn key depending on your method of deployment. For one, the actual "IncusOS" deployments are really particular about having a newer version of TPM (not something the old boxes I purchase typically have). So you are still likely to install something like Debian + incus-cli tools. 

Once you have your distro + incus package setup though, there are a few things you have to tackle. For one, if you actually want separate IP addresses per VM (or LXC) you'll likely need to solve the chicken and egg problem with macvlan, otherwise you'll have to figure out something for a reverse proxy with the network bridge.

So because I was pressed against the wall (my family was irritated about no jellfyin or immich), and I knew that I didn't want to do LXCs again and simply wanted to do most things I can in containers, I went the podman route instead. 

Every app gets it's own local user. You can install podman-compose, and use the same commands as docker compose basically to get your app up. All rootless, and you can also setup podman compose apps with daemons so that they start on boot: https://www.it-hure.de/2024/02/podman-compose-and-systemd/. If you don't care about rootless isolation, I think Docker is still fine. Everyone seems to make documentation and build their apps with it in mind still. 

I still had a need for VMs, so now I just use the standard Qemu+KVM+libvirtd combo for the one or two apps that need that need a full on separation from other apps. 

All of it is in Ansible playbooks now, and I'm pretty happy with the setup I think.

TL; DR

Incus is really cool. I probably wouldn't bother with IncusOS on old hardware, I'd just install a standard Linux distro + incus packages. Spend your time evaluating it (and making it infrastructure code for easy deployment maintenance). Maybe try out the other "standard" ways to do it instead to compare (Docker, Podman, Qemu+KVM, etc).

In a nutshell, doing it this way adds robustness when -- not if -- the destination software changes its behavior, inadvertently or not. It's very similar to software assertions: if this assumption stops holding, then we want to know ASAP because it means subsequent logic is no longer valid.

In the Immich case, the author writes:

> This is a side effect of how Immich checks permissions, not a feature made for this purpose, so a future version of Immich could change it. If this ever changes, the share links will answer 404 and I will notice quickly.

Suppose the author updates their Immich instance but missed a remark in the release notes that share keys will be using a different hash algorithm. That's a mistake with their upgrade procedure, sure, but it'd be ideal if such mistakes were detected sooner than later. Without the check for link validity, the only log that would record the now-invalid share links would be in Immich logs. But with this additional check, there is also a log at Caddy. More visibility, combined with an existing alerting regime, means errors and mistakes are captured earlier.

At first glance, it might seem like both approaches still result in a 404 for the user, which suggests neither approach is really "robust". But one is a near-silent failure yet the other gives a loud, unmistakable signal that something is broken, meaning it can be addressed. Phrased another way, the signal-to-noise ratio of an assert fail is very strong.

> I'd prefer a compact, reasonably power-efficient, ready-made NAS rather than building a full PC, mostly due to limited space.

This goes against your preference for open software, because all ready-made compact NAS appliances will come with proprietary software and proprietary hardware... because that's their business model, tying you to their products.

Regarding power, you're not saving as much as you think when you consider that the HDDs will take the lion's share. It doesn't really matter if the base system consumes 4W or 20W in idle if the HDDs consume 15W/drive.

If you're an experienced PC builder this is a no-brainer. Building a PC lets you replace components separately and get away with buying used and off-the-shelf.

Choose a case with the right amount of (dampened) HDD cages (I prefer Fractal Design but there are others) and a quality power supply. The motherboard should also have an appropriate amount of SATA connectors. The CPU is not terribly important and can be a decade old. In fact you can get away with buying a used kit. You don't need a lot of RAM, even 8 GB will do (but if you can get 16 or 32 that's nice too). Same for the system SSD, it can be as low as 64 GB or even lower. 

> How much hardware performance do I actually need?

Depends if you have specialized usage. For example if you want to do AI on the CPU. Or if you want to do video transcoding. If you don't, anything will do.

> Which software stack would you recommend?

A dedicated CalDAV/CardDAV server for contacts and calendar/tasks. Radicale and Baikal are the most popular.

Immich for photo organization (albums, sharing, face recog, semantic search) and photo backup. Basically it was designed to be a great Google Photos replacement.

Personally I would avoid Nextcloud, it's a beast. I would definitely not tie important stuff like calendars into it. Strictly for files may wanna look at alternatives like Seafile or OpenCloud.

For file sync most people use Syncthing but I don't like their mobile (non-official) support. Personally I prefer FolderSync + SSH.

If you get into media libraries then Jellyfin can cover video, audio and books too, but there are also other specialized ones for music and books.

> What should I consider regarding backups and remote access?

Not sure why you're conflating these two.

For remote access if you're not behind CGNAT at the ISP then VPN (Wireguard or OpenVPN) and/or SSH is the most secure.

Tailscale is a good alternative, it works behind CGNAT too, and it has a bunch of other interesting features like exit nodes. Look into it. It's a "mesh VPN" that uses open source clients with a central server that facilitates the pairing from behind NAT. The connections themselves are always private.

If you have to expose HTTP services over the Internet you **must** get a domain, reverse proxy, HTTPS certificates (with auto-renewal, most reverse proxies will help with this) and mTLS is the best security option. But keep in mind very few mobile apps support mTLS (Immich, DAVx5, Ntfy do).

For backups, first of all use a proper backup tool like Borg or Restic, not sync tools like Rsync. You want your backup tool to offer integrity checks, recovery, encryption, deduplication and compression, sync tools offer almost none of these.

Secondly, look into 3-2-1 backup strategy. Affordable backup methods for home use include backup "cold" HDDs, Blu Ray optical discs, and online storage subscriptions. Borg/Restic include support for transparent online backups too.

You don't have to backup *everything*. Categorize your data and figure out some priorities. Usually the truly important data is not very large.

RAID and other forms of storage redundancy are NOT backup, they're mostly about keeping services going during drive failures. If you have to work with limited amount of drives I would prioritize backup over redundancy.

**EMAIL:**

You don't have to self-host the sending and receiving of email to retain control over it. It's in fact very hard to do that.

What you need is to choose a good domain for your @ addresses, on a long-lasting TLD (preferably an EU ccTLD, perhaps your own country's), and an email provider (see the link at the top) that offers SMTP and IMAP without any shenanigans.

You can use IMAP to sync your online mailboxes constantly at home, and also use IMAP to check your online mailbox with any email client, and use the provider's SMTP to send mail. Any decent provider will supply you with the DNS records that need to go into your domain setup so you can use them.

If you ever want to switch provider it's as simple as signing up with another and changing your DNS records.

You _can_ if you want self-host an IMAP server and a webmail client at home on top of your local email archive, so you can search through old emails, and so you can delete them from the online mailbox so you can reduce your online mailbox size (and perhaps pay less). Just as long as you don't try to self-host the ability to send and receive.

Other things you might want to look for at a provider is alias capability, or at least a catch-all. Helps a lot if you give each different online account its own different email address, and never give out your real address (the one you use to login to the email server).

Most email providers will tax you per mailbox and for things like aliases. IMO that's bullcrap. Personally I prefer a provider that allows for unlimited mailboxes and aliases and taxes for tiers of storage space and emails sent/received. Migadu is one such European example. For two people YMMV, either model might be ok. When you have more than two accounts the unlimited model can become much cheaper very fast.

**Things you may not have considered:**

Look into a reverse proxy and getting a domain + HTTPS certificates for it, and putting your services behind it at addresses such as `https://cal.example.com/`. It will make your service consumption 100x better.

Also consider your home router. Is it a capable one? Most people overlook this completely, but a good router can help immensely with self-hosting for things like DNS, VLANs, port forwarding, having stable IPs for servers etc. You can flash a cheap router with OpenWRT and get excellent features out of it.

If you need notifications, or sending messages+attachments across devices, or action buttons, Ntfy can either be self-hosted or used through their public service.

It sounds like you just wants Nextcloud and maybe Immich. So here’s my suggestion:

If you don’t have a domain yet, buy a domain. Preferably through Cloudflare because their API is good, and you’ll need that. Point an apex A record at your public IP address.

Set up something like Kubuntu on the box itself. Make sure it has a static IP address (you can also do DHCP reserved through your router, which is safer), and forward ports 80 (TCP), 443 (TCP), and 51820 (UDP) to that box.

Now comes the magic. Install docker through the official installation docs for Ubuntu (don’t use Ubuntu’s packages). Create a folder in your home directory called “services”. Inside this folder, you’re going to set up a folder for each service you need. The first one you should set up is “nginx-proxy-manager”. Inside each folder you’ll have a “docker-compose.yml” file. Inside that file, set up your docker compose stack. Nginx Proxy Manager’s is pretty simple. Just one service. But change the network mode to “host” (`network_mode: host`), and remove the ports section.

https://nginxproxymanager.com/setup/

Now, from a terminal, in that folder, run `docker compose up -d`. Get used to that command, you’ll run it a lot. Then go to localhost:81, and create an account for NPM. Use a real email address, because that’ll be your contact email for Let’s Encrypt ssl. Go into the ssl settings and create a certificate. You’ll need an api key from Cloudflare, or whatever other place you bought your domain from. It needs access to change the dns settings for your domain. Use this format to create your certificate:

`example.com, *.example.com`

And use the dns challenge option where you’ll put your api key.

# Important Edit:

One thing I forgot to mention, don’t use Docker volumes. Use a bind mount to mount a real directory inside the folder. It should look something like this:

```
    volumes:
      ./data:/data
```

**NOT** like this:

```
    volumes:
      data:/data
```

That way, when you back up that folder, it backs up all your data with it. If you use a docker volume (the one without the “./“), you’ll need to back those up separately. This is important for all of the mounts on every one of your services, especially the database services.

Immich has so many dirs and files that it will take hour/hours for any file-based program to walk that tree (on an HDD) in order to do a backup. I used to use rsync, syncthing, duplicity and had gotten it to about under an hour for 1TB library. The service has to be shutdown to preserve consistency of the backup. So that downtime was okay once per day. Still a heavy operation. Not great, not terrible.

Because of the above you might want to do one of the following:
- Use snapshotting filesystem like ZFS or Btrfs. That allows to avoid the downtime as you can backup a frozen-in-time snapshot while Immich is running.
- The above but with ZFS om both the Immich end and the backup end. That allows transferring just the delta between the new Immich snapshot and the last snapshot the backup has. This happens entirely within the filesystem so there are no file operations needed. At every point in time ZFS knows what blocks have changed between now and the previously backed up snapshot. When you ask it for that, it starts spitting data without spensing an hour figuring out what changed. That allows online backups every hour or even more frequently. The backup of my 1TB Immich instance (HDD) takes 5-10 seconds to initiate the network transfer, then it takes whatever time it takes to get to the backup machine, which is usually equivalent to transferring whatever new was stored in Immich.

So depending on how painful migrations are for you, I'd highly recommend the latter. Otherwise the former. The ZFS snapshot send strategy works for any service you may run.

If you end up running it headless (game streaming host, Jellyfin/Immich worker, whatever), two small things save a lot of hassle:

- Get an HDMI dummy plug (a "display emulator", a few euros). With no internal panel detected and nothing on HDMI, the GPU often has no proper display to render to, and Sunshine/Steam streaming in particular wants a "real" display to capture at the resolution you pick.
- Check the BIOS for a "power on after AC loss" / "auto power on" option. Plenty of laptops don't have it, but if yours does, it comes back on its own after an outage like a proper server. Otherwise Wake-on-LAN from one of your mini PCs is the fallback.

And since storage is your bottleneck right now, open it up and see if there's a second M.2 slot. Some of these chassis have one, and then it could hold some data while also taking the Immich/Paperless ML jobs on the 3050Ti.

My first thought would be to try and fix it, then you have a nice laptop or get to be the family hero when you return it working to your brother. 

Past that there are several services you might use that can take advantage of the video card: Immich image recognition, Paperless OCR, some of the local Whisper servers. 

Or you have a nice set-top PC for big screen gaming and media playback.

Here’s my take on your questions:

1. Doesn’t matter at all where you get a domain. Pick any reliable registrar where the price is right. 
2. The top-level domain (TLD) is the domain name’s suffix and you can use any that you like. Some cost more than others, so you may want to compare prices. 
3. To start with, anything from within the past 10-15 years should be good enough. There are trade-offs, though. Older machines may use more power, for example, but don’t get hung up on details at this point. Get something cheap like an old laptop with an Ethernet port and you’ll be good to go. Once you’ve done it for a while, you’ll understand any downsides and the next piece of hardware you get will be an even better informed choice. 
4. Not at all. Self host as much as you want, but I’d recommend starting slowly. Pick one thing and set it up on your server. Tweak it until it’s just how you want it, makes backups, test. Then add the next thing. Immich, forgejo, and a website are nice easy ones to start with. Communications platforms like chat apps and email are much more involved. Maybe save those for slightly later. 
5. For sure! You can use any OS you’d like. I’ll mention that a lot of the very basic tutorials will assume you’re using Ubuntu or Debian, both of which use systemd. For Devuan, for example, you could mostly follow those same tutorials, but you’ll have to fill in some of the blanks. I’ll mention that Linux isn’t the only option, either. If you don’t like systemd, you might enjoy something like FreeBSD. It sounds from your experience like you’ll be able to handle this part. 

Whatever you do, just remember that it doesn’t need to be perfect immediately. You’re going to mess a bunch of things up and make decisions you’ll wish you hadn’t. You’ll spend a lot of time destroying and recreating things you’ve already done. That’s the joy of self-taught self hosting!

It works but I wouldn't call it the cleanest solution, more a workaround. As far as I know only apps targeting SDK 37 are affected, older apps still get the permission implicitly. So the proper way would be to just grant "Nearby devices" to the apps that need it e.g. Immich or Jellyfin and if an app doesn't ask for it that's actually a bug and worth reporting, because it should request the permission as soon as the server resolves to a local IP. I also find the "Nearby Devices" title a bit misleading for apps that only need it to reach your own server, but on the other side it gives a somehow proper hint what the permission actually allows.

Proxmox exclusively with unprivileged LXCs, which themselves host other docker containers/stacks managed with Dockhand (a more modern alternative to both Portainer and Dockge). I have a very tiny low power machine so I have to be kind with my resources, therefore no VMs. But LXCs are simpler anyway. I can easily pass devices like `/dev/tun` for tailscale and i forget the name of the iGPU for accelerated workloads (for Immich, Nextcloud).

Reasoning: with containers it's easy to make mistakes without dire consequences (just `docker compose down -v` and start over). The LXCs are easy to back up and restore. They hold internal running state of whatever docker containers I run in them.

Pro tip: don't map host paths using the UI (`mp0` etc), use `lxc.mount` instead. This will let you continue to have snapshots of your LXCs whereas the other approach makes your LXC incompatible with snapshots.

Good luck!

That said, make sure you also invest the time and energy into a proper 3-2-1 backup strategy:
* 3 copies: your primary pool of data (Immich library) and at least two backup copies
* 2 different media types: SSD/NVMe as well as HDD NAS (as an example)
* 1 copy off-site: cloud backup and/or another server located at a friend's house

How I do it:
* Immich lives on my Unraid server which is 3x14TB spinning HDDs (two arrray disks and one parity)
* NIghtly backup to another small server in same physical area as Unraid server but using NVMe storage
* Nightly backup to yet another small server with NVMe storage at a family members house
* Nightly backup to Backblaze B2 storage

Many of them were to test which I wanted for a specified purpose (miniflux vs selfoss for rss, lychee vs photoprism for pictures, etc). Without yunohost, these programs would have been inaccessible to me. And in the process, I have learned a few things about yunohost. Most programs install to subdomains so you have have a number of programs installed on the same system, but some programs MUST be installed to the main domain. And I never could get those to install if I already had programs installed to subdomains. Those programs would need to be installed first, THEN you could install the rest after it got its main domain spot. Not easy to to figure out unless you know that ahead of time. Also, if two programs you need both require the main domain, you can only have one; that is, unless you set up a second domain in yunohost. Then you could install both as the main in each domain. I haven't tried that, but I have tried moving installed programs from one domain to a different one and everything worked well. I have upgraded yunohost to new versions and things worked well, and I have upgraded the programs and that also worked smoothly; EXCEPT for one time with nextcloud. Several years ago, the nextcloud upgrade broke something about the database and I had to reinstall it. But I've also used TrueNAS on an old computer and installed nextcloud with it before and it also broke nextcloud, so that seems to be something I have to worry about with that specific program... Anyway, I love yunohost and would recommend it. 

I actually tried out CasaOS this year. I've heard a lot about docker and CasaOS and figured I'd play with it and see how it is. It worked well when I installed my programs on it. It doesn't have as large a list as yunohost, but the ones it had worked well. My hope was that since it used docker, I could install other programs packed with docker on it as well, which would ovecome the smaller store. I have run photoprism straight from mdadm RAID5 on some ye olde SAS drives with only a reduction in the indexing speed (About 30K photos which took ~2 hours to index with GPU tensorflow).

That being said I'm in a similar boat doing an upgrade and I have some warnings that I have found are helpful:

1. Consumer grade NVMEs are not designed for tons of write ops, so they should optimally only be used in RAID 0/1/10. RAID 5/6 will literally start with a massive parity rip on the drives, and the default timer for RAID checks on Linux is 1 week. Same goes for ZFS and mdadm caching, just proceed with caution (ie 321 backups) if you go that route. Even if you end up doing RAID 5/6, make sure you get quality hardware with decent TBW, as sever grade NVMEs are often triple in TBW rating.
2. ZFS is a load of pain if you're running anything related to Fedora or Redhat, and the performance implications from lots and lots of testing is still arguably inconclusive on a NAS/Home lab setup. Unless you rely on the specific feature set or are making an actual hefty storage node, stock mdadm and LVM will probably fulfill your needs.
3. Btrfs has all the features you need but is a load of trash in performance, highly recommend XFS for file integrity features + built in data dedup, and mdadm/lvm for the rest.

I'm personally going with the NVME scheduled backups to RAID because the caching just doesn't seem worth it when I'm gonna be slamming huge media files around all day along with running VMs and other crap. For context, the 2TB NVME brand I have is only rated for 1200 TBW. That's probably more then enough for a file server, but for my homelab server it would just be caching constantly with whatever workload I'm throwing at it. Would still probably last a few years no issues, but SSD pricing has just been awful these past few years.

On a related note, Photoprism needs to upgrade to Tensorflow 2 so I don't have to compile an antiquated binary for CUDA support.

Both your RAID and NVMe data should be getting backed up daily to 2 different destinations, if it's irreplaceable.

But to answer your question, just place the DB and cache files for Photoprism on the NVMe, and the photos themselves on the RAID.

So, in thinking about this in more concrete terms (as opposed to vague dissatisfaction), I suspect what we really want is a blogging platform with robust authenticated reader interaction tools.

The issue with AP, and therefore most of these servers, is that (a) it's expected to be public by default (the privacy point you mention), but almost more fundamentally (b) they're aggregators. People either to a bunch of people and get a feed of a bunch of posts by different people (Mastodon/X); or they join a community and see a bunch of posts by different people (Lemmy/Reddit).

I think what we want is blogging software, with an endless stream of content posted by a single user, but with reactions and threaded conversations per post. I've been thinking how this could be achieved on various AP platforms, but while you can almost get there with groups/channels/communities, the sticking point is that they are all ultimately designed around any member being able to post top-level content. > how do I sync my notes/photos/files/etc to the “cloud” of GrapheneOS?

GrapheneOS doesn't have a cloud. You need to find a solution for syncing your data yourself. There's [DAVx5](https://f-droid.org/packages/at.bitfire.davdroid/), which uses the WebDAV protocol, [Nextcloud](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.nextcloud.client), [EteSync](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.etesync.syncadapter), [PhotoPrism](https://www.photoprism.app/), [Immich](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/app.alextran.immich) and many more. They all serve different purposes. DAVx5 works with any WebDAV-compatible server, it lets you sync calendars, contacts and tasks. Nextcloud is a self-hosted replacement for things like Google Drive, it lets you sync files, calendars, contacts, notes, photos, bookmarks, recipies, basically everything you could imagine. Note that the official Nextcloud app only lets you sync files, but there are [other Nextcloud-compatible apps on F-Droid](https://search.f-droid.org/?q=nextcloud&lang=en) that let you use more features of the Nextcloud server. Both PhotoPrism and Immich are self-hosted solutions for syncing your photos, [Immich has an official Android app on F-Droid ](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/app.alextran.immich), PhotoPrism only has this unofficial one called Gallery for [PhotoPrism](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/ua.com.radiokot.photoprism). If you're not into self-hosting, there are still good, private options out there. [EteSync](https://www.etesync.com/) allows you to sync your contacts, calendars, tasks and notes, and it uses end-to-end encryption by default. You can self-host it, but you don't have to. You can just pay them $2/month and they will handle it for you. Personally, I like to self-host my own instance of [Etebase](https://www.etebase.com/), the backend server for EteSync. Other private, cloud-hosted options are [Proton](https://proton.me/) for email, calendar and files or [Ente](https://ente.io/) for photos ([their app is also on F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/io.ente.photos.fdroid)).
